title: Iterating on LLM apps at scale  Learnings from Discord: Ian Webster

summary: Ian Webster, a Senior Staff Engineer at Discord and maintainer of the open-source Promptfoo evaluation tool, recounts lessons from shipping LLM products at Discord's scale. The flagship product was Clyde AI, a chatbot launched to over 200 million users. Webster emphasizes that the hardest challenges were not models, fine-tuning, or product design, but safety: preventing harmful outputs like instructions for building weapons, harassment, and racism. Security, legal, safety, and policy stakeholders were the biggest repeat launch blockers. At Discord's scale, even a one-in-a-million failure occurs roughly 200 times. Webster's central thesis is that evaluations should be treated as simple unit tests: fast, deterministic, locally runnable, and unintimidating. A concrete example: to encourage a casual chat personality, Discord simply checked that outputs began with a lowercase letter—getting 80% of the value for 1% of the effort. For retrieval-augmented web search, he recommends splitting evals into triggering logic and static-context summarization tests. Key trade-offs include cost versus accuracy and the diminishing returns from over-specifying prompts. Prompts are a form of vendor lock-in since GPT-style prompts don't transfer cleanly to Claude or Llama. He stresses building an eval culture where developers run dozens of evals per day and every PR includes an eval. For observability, Discord used Datadog rather than LLM-specific tools. Privacy constraints prevented closing the live feedback loop, so the team relied on dogfooding and public reports. A notable routing trick: for lower-powered models drifting from system prompts, randomly injecting GPT-4 responses acted as a corrective 'bowling alley bumper.' The talk concludes with an in-depth look at red teaming. Webster himself was victim of the 'grandma jailbreak' that originated on Discord, where Clyde AI was tricked into providing a Napalm recipe by role-playing as a deceased grandmother. He identifies two safeguarding schools: predeployment (risk assessment, red teaming, compliance) and live filtering, arguing predeployment is most important. Promptfoo includes a risk assessment view categorizing brand risk, legal risk, and other dimensions. Discord used unaligned models to generate toxic test inputs automatically. Beyond basic harmful input testing, they discovered application-specific jailbreaks introduced by custom prompts, using a feed-forward loop where an attacker LLM sends adversarial inputs and a judge guides rewording via euphemisms and synonyms to bypass safeguards. Additional failure modes covered include PII leaks, hallucination, hijacking (e.g., using the bot for homework), and political opinions.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and background
sections.summary: Ian introduces himself as a Senior Staff Engineer at Discord, maintainer of Promptfoo, and leader of teams that shipped LLM products at Discord scale. He previews a speedrun of lessons learned.

sections.title: Clyde AI and the safety challenge at scale
sections.summary: Discord shipped Clyde AI, a chatbot to over 200 million users. The hardest challenge was not models or fine-tuning but preventing harmful outputs like bomb-making instructions. Security, legal, safety, and policy were the biggest repeat launch blockers. At scale, one-in-a-million failures happen 200 times.

sections.title: Evals philosophy: treat as simple unit tests
sections.summary: Evals should be treated like unit tests: fast, deterministic, and local. Example: encouraging casual chat personality by checking that output starts with a lowercase letter—80% of the value for 1% of the effort.

sections.title: RAG eval architecture
sections.summary: For web search with retrieval and generation, split evals into triggering logic tests and static-context summarization tests, rather than hooking into live databases or live web searches.

sections.title: Trade-offs: cost, accuracy, and prompt specificity
sections.summary: Cost versus accuracy trade-offs across models. Over-specifying prompts yields diminishing then negative returns—less is more. Prompts are a form of vendor lock-in; GPT-style prompts don't transfer cleanly to Claude or Llama.

sections.title: Building an eval culture
sections.summary: Evals should run locally without cloud dependencies, use simple deterministic metrics, and be easy enough for devs to run dozens per day. Every PR should include an eval link or CI/CD integration. Discord built Promptfoo as a local CLI for declarative eval configs.

sections.title: Observability and the feedback loop
sections.summary: Discord used Datadog for LLM observability rather than specialized tools—best observability tool is the one already in use. Did some online model-graded evals fed into Datadog. Could not close the live feedback loop due to privacy constraints; relied on dogfooding and public reports of failures and wins.

sections.title: Prompt management and model routing
sections.summary: Used Git for prompt versioning and Retool for non-technical configuration. For lower-powered models drifting from system prompts in long conversations, randomly injecting GPT-4 responses acted as a corrective 'bowling alley bumper.'

sections.title: Red teaming: jailbreaks and adversarial testing
sections.summary: Discord's largely teenage user base exists to break and abuse LLMs. Ian was victim of the 'grandma jailbreak' that originated on Discord, tricking Clyde AI into giving Napalm recipes. Two safeguarding approaches: predeployment (risk assessment, red teaming, compliance/legal) and live filtering, with predeployment being most important. Promptfoo includes a risk assessment view categorizing brand risk, legal risk, and other dimensions. Discord used unaligned models to auto-generate toxic test inputs. Beyond basic harmful input testing, application-specific prompts introduce new jailbreak vectors. A feed-forward attacker-judge loop—where an attacker LLM sends adversarial inputs and a judge guides rewording via euphemisms and synonyms—successfully exposed cracks in safeguards. Additional failure modes include PII leaks, hallucination, hijacking (e.g., homework), and political opinions. Promptfoo is open source.
